doc.title: Eddie Metz Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, October 3, 2015

chapter: College and the road to jazz
title: Declining Berklee and starting business school
summary: Accepted to Berklee with a full ride in 1976, he stays in Michigan at Eastern Michigan as a marketing major while gigging.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: You had a path, like you were going to go into business or something?

Oh yeah. I graduated high school in Ann Arbor, Michigan in 1976 and was accepted at Berklee College of Music in Boston, and placed in the number three big band as a freshman. That was like what? Okay. I guess I’m pretty good at what I’m doing here, and I’d love to go to Berklee and be a musician. And my dad was a musician, never a full time musician. He was an investment banker and kept the food on the table. He could have been a professional musician had he gone that way but he decided not to. He was raised a different way. And so when I decided to go into music he was like, “I don’t think so” — even with an acceptance to Berklee with a full ride. And I didn’t go. I’m not going to say it’s a regret, but I wonder where my career might have gone if I’d gone in that direction. So that was 1976. Instead I stayed in Ann Arbor. I didn’t go to the University of Michigan, I went to Eastern Michigan, five miles down the road, in Ypsilanti, Michigan. And I was in business school. I was a marketing major for three years. So the first year was easy, you get algebra 101 and psychology 101 and English 101. When you get to the second year and you get things like business law and business classes, how to

write a letter in the proper business form with the headings and all of that stuff, and memos, and all of that stuff you need to do when you’re in business. And I started going like I don’t know if this is for me. And then in the meantime I’m still in my hometown playing gigs Friday and Saturday nights. Now I didn’t hang out with the guys in the dorms, I went and played gigs. I was making 75 bucks a night as a college student. You know 150 bucks a week. I bought pizza for everybody. Because I was in the dorms. And so I was in college just partying out and having a good old time, playing my gigs and being in the marching band and being in the concert band and being in the jazz band at Eastern Michigan, and eventually I just stopped going to my academic classes. I went to the music classes. And I became a huge pothead. It was the 70s, it was the thing to do.
You’re diving into the whole thing.
